FB_2018q1.summary_analysis: This Heard on the Street column examines Facebook's fourth-quarter 2017 results through the lens of CEO Mark Zuckerberg's stated 2018 goal of 'fixing' the social network, including an overhaul of the News Feed and video efforts, which he had warned could hurt usage since 'protecting our community is more important than maximizing our profit.' The column finds Zuckerberg 'half right' so far: usage did take a real hit, with daily active users reaching 1.4 billion, up only 2.4% sequentially -- the lowest sequential growth on record for that metric and down sharply from 4.1% growth a year earlier -- and the 33 million net new daily users added in the quarter came in below the 46 million Wall Street analysts had expected. Yet the article stresses that the financial results told the opposite story: revenue jumped 47% year over year to just under $13 billion, operating income surged 61% to $7.4 billion, and Facebook wasn't cutting spending to protect margins either, with 2017 capital expenditures soaring 49% to $6.7 billion. The column adds a comparative data point on profitability, noting that on a trailing twelve-month basis Facebook generates about 50 cents of operating profit per dollar of revenue, roughly twice the margin of megacap peers Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet. The piece's forward-looking conclusion is explicitly cautionary rather than descriptive of the quarter itself: it argues investors should 'get ready for a slightly less profitable Facebook' once the more significant product changes -- and their effects on advertisers -- are fully reflected in future results.
FB_2018q1.why_moved: As a Heard on the Street opinion column, the piece does not report an after-hours trading reaction or attribute the stock's actual multi-day move to any specific figure; it instead lays out the tension between a clear engagement miss (33 million new daily users versus the 46 million analysts expected, the slowest sequential DAU growth on record) and record financial strength (47% revenue growth, 61% operating income growth) without stating which side the market weighted more heavily. Given that the stock rose over the following days, it is a reasonable inference that investors leaned toward the financial-strength side of that split described above rather than the engagement slowdown, but the article itself offers no explicit statement connecting its content to the specific positive price reaction -- it stays focused on warning that the true financial cost of Zuckerberg's 'fixing Facebook' agenda has not yet arrived, a caution about the future rather than an explanation of the immediate move.

FB_2018q2.summary_analysis: Described in the article as Facebook's 'first snapshot' of how the Cambridge Analytica data-privacy scandal was affecting its underlying business, the first-quarter 2018 report showed earnings per share of $1.69 versus $1.04 a year earlier, revenue up nearly 50% to $11.97 billion, and net income up 63% to nearly $5 billion from $3.06 billion -- results the article says 'topped analyst expectations.' Monthly active users grew by about 70 million to 2.2 billion, and the company announced an additional $9 billion in share buybacks on top of a previously authorized $6 billion. The scandal itself is described in detail: Cambridge Analytica, which aided the Trump campaign in 2016, allegedly obtained data on tens of millions of Facebook users from an outside developer, sparking a #deletefacebook backlash and prompting Zuckerberg to testify before Congress twice earlier in the month. On the earnings call, COO Sheryl Sandberg directly addressed the central investor question, stating the company hadn't seen a 'meaningful trend' of advertisers fleeing the platform; Merkle's Andy Taylor is quoted saying major advertisers were aware of the controversy and in a 'wait-and-see mode' but had not made significant moves, contrasting this relatively muted reaction with the more damaging backlash Alphabet's YouTube had faced over ad placement next to objectionable content. The article also flags real forward risk: CFO David Wehner warned that European user growth could go flat or decline once new GDPR privacy rules take effect in May, and most analysts and investors, per the piece, believe additional regulation is 'inevitable,' with Zuckerberg telling lawmakers he was open to some regulation but wary of rules that could hinder U.S. companies competing against Chinese rivals.
FB_2018q2.why_moved: Facebook shares rose about 7% in after-hours trading, and the article frames this explicitly as a relief rally: shares had fallen more than 18% from a record high in early February heading into the report, reflecting investor fear that the Cambridge Analytica fallout described above would visibly damage the ad business, but the 50% revenue growth and 63% net income growth, combined with Sandberg's direct statement that no 'meaningful trend' of advertiser defection had emerged, addressed that fear head-on. The contrast the article draws with Alphabet -- which beat its own first-quarter expectations the same week but saw shares fall 4.8%, its worst session in more than two months, on separate expense concerns -- reinforces that Facebook's rally was specifically about the market concluding the privacy scandal had not yet dented the underlying advertising business, even as the piece is careful to note that much of the Cambridge Analytica fallout happened after the quarter closed in March and that the looming GDPR-driven European user risk flagged by Wehner remained an unresolved overhang.

The results themselves were mixed rather than uniformly weak: earnings per share of $1.74 edged past the $1.72 analyst consensus, but revenue of $13.23 billion missed the $13.36 billion analysts had expected, according to Thomson Reuters -- the company's first revenue miss since the first quarter of 2015, as the article specifically notes. Management layered a pointed deceleration warning on top of that miss: executives said the revenue growth rate had already fallen seven percentage points quarter over quarter and would decrease by 'high single-digit percentages' in the second half of 2018, while guiding operating margins down from the quarter's 44% to the 'mid-30s' over the next several years due to higher product and infrastructure spending. User trends in lucrative markets also softened: daily active users in the U.S. and Canada were flat at 185 million, while European daily users slipped to 279 million from 282 million, a decline executives attributed to the new European GDPR privacy law taking effect during the quarter. Zuckerberg himself called the results 'another solid quarter' on the call, but the article notes those comments were 'quickly overshadowed' when other executives detailed the growth deceleration and margin guidance, with SocialFlow CEO Jim Anderson quoted wondering whether the results signaled 'an early warning sign that the market's assumptions about tech companies' growth failed to account for the fact that each of us only has 24 hours in a day.'
FB_2018q3.why_moved: The article ties the record plunge directly to the specific combination established above: a rare revenue miss against consensus -- the first since early 2015 -- landing alongside an explicit management warning that revenue growth would keep decelerating by high single digits through the back half of 2018 and that operating margins would compress from 44% toward the mid-30s for years to come. That the softness showed up specifically in Europe, where daily active users actually declined and where executives linked the drop to new GDPR rules, gave the deceleration warning concrete, near-term evidence rather than leaving it as an abstract caution, which the article suggests amplified the market's reaction. Zuckerberg's own characterization of the quarter as 'another solid quarter,' delivered just before the more cautious guidance from his fellow executives took over the narrative, underscores the article's framing that it was the forward-looking guidance and the rare revenue miss -- not the past quarter's underlying growth of 42% -- that investors reacted to so severely.

The 'abrupt reversal' on capital needs -- guiding capital expenditures 50% higher just months after saying no capital raise would be necessary -- combined with the eyebrow-raising use of Model 3 deposits to pay down a credit line, gave the column concrete reasons to argue that Musk's more ambitious 2018 goals deserved 'thorough scrutiny' rather than celebration, a skeptical framing consistent with the stock's decline despite the narrow quarterly beat.

Our issue is we can't do that.' Hackett's 'fitness' plan targets $14 billion in cumulative cost cuts through 2022 by simplifying engineering, manufacturing and model lineups, including a signaled retreat from sedans toward trucks and SUVs. Deutsche Bank analyst Rod Lache said, 'Ford's strategy will take several years to bear fruit,' and Evercore ISI noted 'the performance gap between the two [Ford and GM] appears to continue to widen.' F_2018q2.summary_analysis: Ford's first-quarter 2018 results, reported April 25, 2018, showed the company committing to hit an 8% profit-margin target two years earlier than previously planned, reflecting CEO Jim Hackett's push for more aggressive cost action, including pulling unprofitable small cars from U.S. dealerships so trucks and SUVs eventually make up 90% of sales volume; the company confirmed it will only continue selling the Mustang and a crossover version of the Focus domestically, eliminating the Fusion, Taurus and Fiesta. Net profit rose 9% to $1.7 billion on a lower corporate tax rate; operating profit fell 13% to $2.2 billion as weaker North American results and Asia-Pacific losses offset improved Ford Credit performance. Ford raised its planned cumulative cost cuts to $25.5 billion by 2022 from a prior $14 billion target, including a $5 billion reduction in capital spending, with CFO Bob Shanks saying, 'Everything will be on the table. F_2018q3.summary_analysis: Ford's second-quarter 2018 results, reported July 25, 2018, showed net income dropping 48% and the company lowering its 2018 profit outlook, citing tariff-related commodity cost pressures and weakness in Asia and Europe; it also outlined a broad multiyear restructuring that could bring $11 billion in charges. Net income of $1.1 billion was hurt by about $300 million in higher year-over-year commodity costs, nearly half tied to U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs, which CFO Bob Shanks said could shave up to $600 million off full-year profit; Shanks called it 'obviously a very tough quarter for us.' China sales sank 26% in the first half of the year, and the China business swung to a $483 million operating loss from a $23 million profit a year earlier, which Shanks attributed to a stale product lineup hurting both volumes and pricing. Adjusted EPS of 27 cents missed the 31-cent analyst consensus; revenue fell 2% to $38.9 billion. Results were also hurt by nearly $600 million from a truck-production disruption after a parts-supplier outage idled Ford's truck plants for more than a week in May. CEO Jim Hackett's restructuring plan, separate from the existing $25.5 billion cost-cutting program, aims to redirect capital toward the most profitable segments, especially the North American truck lineup; Shanks said, 'As we allocate capital to the places we think we can be bigger, better and stronger and away from the areas where we don't think we can get a return, there will be consequences.' The article notes rival GM also cited rising steel costs from the tariffs that took effect June 1 that same day.
